notes.decision: Translated 'the Molding of Man.' Lycopolitan ⲱⲁⲡⲧ corresponds to a verbal noun of fashioning/molding (cf. ϣⲱⲡⲧ̄ 'knead'); the chapter's parallel use of ⲛⲧⲁⲙⲓⲟⲛ 'storehouses' and the broader Manichaean term ⲡⲗⲁⲥⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲧⲙⲛⲧⲣⲱⲙⲉ 'molding of humanity' (already in glossary) confirm this is the technical term for the archonic fashioning/incarnation-form of the human person.

Translated 'ran at' — ⲇⲱⲣⲇ̄ is a verb of pursuit/running with directional ⲁ- 'toward.' Used three times in this passage (lines 11, 14, 24) to describe the cosmic motion of the Molding of Man and the archons toward Matter and toward each other's counsels.

Rendered as appositive: 'Matter, the Enthumesis.' The Greek loan ⲉⲛⲑⲩⲙⲏⲥⲓⲥ here functions cosmologically (the personified Thought of Matter) rather than as the soul's faculty. Cf. accumulated entry on cosmological vs. anthropological uses of ⲉⲛⲑⲩⲙⲏⲥⲓⲥ.

Translated 'has been emptied out.' ⲣ̄-ⲭⲁⲓ̈ⲉ likely from ϫⲁⲉⲓⲉ 'desert, be empty' verbalized; with ⲁⲃⲁⲗ 'forth' = 'made empty out of (something).' The cosmogonic image is that the storehouses of the elements were emptied of their contents into the forming cosmos.

ⲟⲩⲱⲛⲉ left as placeholder — sense uncertain. The simile compares the storehouse of Death to a lake whose fish/birds are hunted while the central depths and plants are left behind. ⲟⲩⲱⲛⲉ might be 'stone' (= petrified place, lair?), 'manifestation' (cf. ⲟⲩⲱⲛⲉ < ⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ̄?), or 'opening.' I have left it untranslated and flagged.

ⲧⲉⲇⲉ here = Sah. ⲧⲱϭⲉ 'plant'; ⲣⲏⲧ 'grow, sprout' (qualitative). The simile completes: just as a hunter takes only fish and birds and leaves middle-depths, others, and growing plants, so the Molding of Man took only some of Death's storehouses and left others behind.

Translated 'limbs.' Lycopolitan term (with characteristic doubled ⲧ) for body-parts; distinct from Greek loan ⲙⲉⲗⲟⲥ ('member') which appears in line 4. The kephalaion's anatomical schema requires three-tiered structure: great limbs (ⲛⲁⲟ̄ ⲛ̄ⲁⲧⲧⲉ) → small wellsprings (ⲛⲓⲕⲟⲩⲓ̄ ⲛ̄ⲁⲛⲝⲱⲭ) → members (ⲙⲉⲗⲟⲥ). Likely related to Coptic ⲁⲧⲉ 'joint' (Crum 17b) or ⲏⲧⲉ 'limb' (Crum 642a) with prosthetic ⲁ-.

Untranslated initial particle/word; possibly trailing element of preceding clause now lost above the line, or a numeric/discourse marker. Left within the Coptic but not represented in English to avoid speculative construction.

Obscure form with overstrokes; tentatively rendered as a deictic-modal particle ('still / yet'). The construction ⲉⲣⲉ ... ⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲉϩⲁⲛⲍ requires a circumstantial reading 'while this man is alive,' and the cosmological-anatomical analogy at lines 25-27 (soul in body) confirms this is the protasis of the alive-state. The exact lexeme remains unidentified.

Read as Lycopolitan circumstantial ⲉϥ-ⲟⲛⲍ̄ 'while he is alive,' with characteristic ⲍ for ϩ in ⲱⲛϩ (cf. accumulated vocab: ⲛⲉⲧⲁⲛⲍ̄ 'the Living Ones,' ⲡⲣⲕⲗⲏⲧⲟⲥ ⲉⲧⲁⲛⲍ̄). The ϩ for circumstantial ⲉϥ- is a known Lyc. orthographic feature.

Read as Lycopolitan reflex of ⲙⲟⲩϫⲧ̄/ⲙⲟⲩⲝⲧ̄ 'mingle, blend' (in glossary as ⲙⲟⲩⲝⲧ̄). The ⲁ-vowel may be a dialectal variant. Together with ⲁⲍⲟⲩⲛ 'inward' yields 'are mingled inward (with him)' — i.e. the great limbs are inwardly intermingled with the body. Fits the cosmological pivot to elements-mingled-in-Hyle's-storehouses.

Translated 'abyss.' Apparent variant or expanded form of ⲡϣⲓⲭϩ 'abyss/pit' (in glossary). The intercalated ⲗ may be scribal or represent a compound (ⲡϣⲓ-ⲗ-ⲭⲍϩ?), but standard Manichaean cosmology places Hyle's storehouses in the ⲡϣⲓⲭϩ before the cosmogonic separation, confirming the abyss-reading.

Read as ⲡⲉⲧ-ⲟⲩ-ⲁϣϩ̄ 'that on which they are hung' — qualitative of ⲁϣⲉ 'hang, suspend.' Resumes line 2 ⲉⲩⲁϣⲉ ... ⲁ-: 'they are hung upon the great limbs.' The thread of the parable: small wellsprings depend on the great limbs as branches depend on the trunk.

Tentatively rendered 'they came-to her.' The verbal form ϣⲁⲛⲟⲩ is unattested in standard glossaries; possibly related to ϣⲱⲛ 'draw near, ail, approach' or a dialectal verb of motion. With directional ⲁⲣⲁⲥ '(directed) at her,' the cosmological narrative requires a motion-verb introducing the moment when the natures' substance was extracted, leading to ⲁⲩⲡⲁⲣⲭⲥ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ 'they were separated forth.'
Read as ⲡⲱⲣⲭ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ 'separate forth' (in glossary as ⲡⲱⲣⲭ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ). Lycopolitan vowel-shift ⲱ→ⲁ in the perfect-passive form ⲁⲩ-ⲡⲁⲣⲭ-ⲥ.

Read as ⲣ̄-ⲁⲣⲅⲟⲛ from Greek ἀργός 'idle, inactive, without-work.' The verbal compound ⲣ̄- + Greek loan = 'become inactive.' The cosmological point: when natures are taken from Hyle's storehouses, the storehouses + elements become 'argon' (without operation) — paralleled at line 23 by 'no energeia came to be in them.' Standard Manichaean physics: ⲉⲛⲉⲣⲅⲓⲁ vs. ⲁⲣⲅⲟⲛ as the active/inactive states.
Read as ⲉ-ⲙⲁⲩⲁ-ⲟⲛ '(while/such that) no longer.' Standard negative+ⲟⲛ 'still/yet' = 'no longer.' The body-without-soul becomes inactive 'no longer' having operation in it.

notes.decision: Translated 'the Death of the Midst, which is the Hyle' — direct correspondential identification: the Manichaean Death-of-the-Midst (the cosmic death-zone) IS Matter. Capitalized 'Death of the Midst' as cosmic principle.
Greek ὕπαρξις 'existence, substance.' Rendered 'an existence' rather than 'a substance' to preserve the more abstract ontological sense; ⲟⲩⲥⲓⲁ is the standard term for 'substance.'

Read as qualitative 'dead' (= ⲙⲟⲟⲩⲧ qualitative), modifying ⲥⲱⲙⲁ. The phrase ⲟⲩⲥⲱⲙⲁ ⲉϩⲙⲁⲩⲧ = 'a body, dead' fits the context of the chapter's discussion of the body of death and the elements without life (line 8).
